1031.quote_or_event: “The True Lord Himself knows all; He makes no mistakes. He is the Great Farmer of the Universe.”
1031.explanation: In Sri Raag, Guru Nanak reaches for the farmer as his image for God Himself: the Creator is the wise cultivator who never errs in sowing and reaping. The verse treats farming as the work most worthy to describe God's own care for the world.
1031.tie_back: The Kural ranks ploughing as the chief of all callings that the whole world finally depends on; Guru Nanak gives the farmer the highest honour possible by naming God the Great Farmer.
1031.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 19, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1031._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the verse exalts farming as an image of God's work rather than arguing, as the Kural does, that every other trade depends on the plough.

1032.quote_or_event: “The farmers love to work their farms; they plow and work the fields, so that their sons and daughters may eat.”
1032.explanation: Guru Ram Das describes the farmer who ploughs with full effort so that his children may be fed, and uses this ordinary devotion as a simile for the devotee's love of the Lord's Name.
1032.tie_back: The Kural calls ploughmen the linchpin that carries everyone who does not till; Guru Ram Das pictures the farmer's toil as what keeps a whole household fed.
1032.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 166, Raag Gauri, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1032._accuracy_note: Good picture of the farmer as provider for dependants, but the scope is a family rather than the whole society, and the line is a simile for devotion.

1033.quote_or_event: “Fareed begs, O Lord, do not make me sit at another's door. If this is the way you are going to keep me, then go ahead and take the life out of my body.”
1033.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, prays that he never be reduced to sitting at someone else's door for his living; he would rather die than live as a dependant.
1033.tie_back: The Kural says only those who eat what they plough truly live, while the rest eat by bowing to others; Farid likewise counts a life spent waiting at another's door as no life at all.
1033.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1380, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 42) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1033._accuracy_note: Strong match on the shame of depending on others for one's bread; Farid does not name farming as the alternative.

1034.quote_or_event: “Dhanna has obtained the Lord, the Sustainer of the World, as his wealth; meeting the humble Saints, he merges in the Lord.”
1034.explanation: Bhagat Dhanna, a Jat farmer whose hymns are in the Guru Granth Sahib, plays on his own name (dhan, wealth) to say that the humble cultivator has gained the greatest wealth of all. On the following page (Ang 488) Guru Arjan notes that the Lord met this Jat in person.
1034.tie_back: The Kural says farmers rich in ripening grain will see many kings' parasols bow under their own king's; Dhanna's verse shows a poor farmer whose true riches outshine any royal treasure.
1034.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 487, Raag Asa, Bhagat Dhanna (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1034._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the link is a farmer whose wealth surpasses kings', but Dhanna's wealth is spiritual and the Kural's point about agrarian prosperity and royal power has no real Sikh counterpart.

1035.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
1035.explanation: In Sarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak contrasts the so-called holy man who goes around begging with the person who earns his food by honest labour and shares part of it. This salok is a classic statement of kirat karni (honest work) and vand chhakna (sharing).
1035.tie_back: The Kural says those who eat by the work of their own hands never beg and give freely to those who do; Guru Nanak names exactly that person, who earns and then gives, as the one who knows the Path.
1035.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Sarang, Sarang ki Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1035._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: earning by one's own labour, not begging, and giving to others are all present; only the specific link to farming is absent.

1036.quote_or_event: “Then Baba (Nanak) returned to Kartarpur where he put aside his attire of a Recluse.”
1036.explanation: Bhai Gurdas records that after his long travels Guru Nanak settled at Kartarpur and laid aside the dress of an udasi (renunciant), living thereafter as a householder among a working community. Bhai Gurdas's Vaaran are early and highly respected exegesis, not scripture.
1036.tie_back: The Kural warns that even those who claim to have renounced all desire cannot survive if the farmers stop work; Guru Nanak's own choice to put off the renunciant's garb and live by settled labour expresses the Sikh preference for the working householder over the dependent ascetic.
1036.source: Bhai Gurdas, Vaar 1, Pauri 38, English translation as given in the BaniDB database
1036._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: it shows the Sikh rejection of renunciation, but does not itself say ascetics depend on farmers; Bhai Gurdas is early exegesis rather than scripture, and the BaniDB translation is unattributed.

1037.quote_or_event: “Let your mind be the farmer; the Lord shall sprout in your heart, and you shall attain the state of Nirvaanaa.”
1037.explanation: Guru Nanak turns the work of cultivation into an image of spiritual discipline: when the mind works like a careful farmer, the Lord sprouts within the heart.
1037.tie_back: The Kural gives a technical rule for preparing soil so that a crop grows abundantly even without manure; Guru Nanak's verse shares only the conviction that well-prepared ground yields a rich harvest, here an inner one.
1037.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 23, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1037._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the Kural's agronomic instruction on drying ploughed soil has no Sikh parallel, and the verse uses farming purely as a spiritual metaphor.

1038.quote_or_event: “Make your mind the farmer, good deeds the farm, modesty the water, and your body the field. Let the Lord's Name be the seed, contentment the plow, and your humble dress the fence.”
1038.explanation: In Sorath, Guru Nanak lays out a full farming routine in spiritual terms, assigning a virtue to each task: tilling, watering, sowing, levelling and fencing the crop against harm.
1038.tie_back: The Kural ranks the farmer's tasks, placing manuring above ploughing and guarding above watering; Guru Nanak likewise lists each stage of farm work, ending with the fence that protects the crop.
1038.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 595, Raag Sorath, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1038._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both walk through the stages of cultivation including guarding the field, but Guru Nanak does not rank the tasks and is speaking allegorically.

1039.quote_or_event: “You work the well and irrigate the fields, but the oxen have already left to graze in the jungle.”
1039.explanation: Guru Ram Das uses the image of a farmer whose oxen have wandered off while he imagines his fields are being watered, as a picture of outward religious effort while the untended mind roams away.
1039.tie_back: The Kural warns that land whose owner stays at home sulks like a neglected wife; Guru Ram Das likewise shows a field that fails because no one is actually tending it.
1039.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 368, Raag Asa, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1039._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the shared idea is that an untended field fails, but the verse is a spiritual allegory and lacks the Kural's image of the land as a sulking wife.

1040.quote_or_event: “Fareed, musk is released at night. Those who are sleeping do not receive their share.”
1040.explanation: Sheikh Farid says the fragrance of grace is handed out in the night hours, and those who lie asleep miss their portion.
1040.tie_back: The Kural says Earth laughs at those who sit idle and complain that they have nothing; Farid likewise says those who sleep through the time of giving go without their share.
1040.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1382, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1040._accuracy_note: Next-best: shares the moral that the idle lose what the diligent receive, but Farid speaks of spiritual wakefulness, not farm labour, and has no image of the Earth laughing.
